Every run from these is post hoc and sits in its own directory; Table 1 is unchanged. | ### 2.2 The system under test A denial arrives with its reason code and the payer's remark. The model is given the payer's written criteria, the denial, the case facts, and the chart, and asked for one of two things: a decision that the record does not support an appeal, with the reason, or a draft in which every sentence carries one citation to one chart entry and a verbatim quote from it. The gate then checks every sentence. If the record does not support an appeal, the software says so instead of arguing anyway. Nothing is sent without a physician's signature. The viewer renders a passing draft as that instrument ([`build/viewer/src/writ.ts`](build/viewer/src/writ.ts)): the payer's reason quoted at the head, each sentence footnoted to the entry, date, and verbatim quote the gate verified it against, the gate version and the input hash at the foot, and a blank signature line under a band that reads draft, unsigned, not sent (Figure 8). It can be printed or saved as text; the page sends nothing. ### 2.3 The fifty cases **What kind of denial.** Every case is a claim denied after the service was given: the payer's remittance, carrying a claim adjustment reason code (CARC) and the payer's remark, for a procedure, admission, drug, or continued stay already delivered. None is a prior-authorization request refused before care. The statistics under The problem are prior-authorization figures because that is where the public record is richest; the response to either kind of denial is the same document, the physician's record read against the payer's written criteria, and the set should be read as a test of that document, not of the prior-authorization process. Thirty-four cases carry CARC 50, not medically necessary. Three carry CARC 197, no authorization on file: in two the plan allows a retrospective medical-necessity review and the chart answers it, and in one the plan refuses that review, so a medical-necessity appeal is the wrong instrument and the right answer is to decline. The rest are experimental or investigational (56), non-covered (96, 167), diagnosis or modifier inconsistent with the procedure (11, 4), frequency (151), benefit maximum (119), and timely filing (29). **How they were made.** The set is generated, not hand-written. [`build/src/synthetic/generate.ts`](build/src/synthetic/generate.ts) builds all fifty deterministically from a fixed seed (20261027) using 18 service templates in [`build/src/synthetic/templates/`](build/src/synthetic/templates/), one per service in the table in [`build/synthetic/README.md`](build/synthetic/README.md), and a test checks that the committed files match the generator, so anyone can regenerate them with `npm run synthetic` and get the same bytes. A fixed plan allocates 30 warranted cases, where the chart documents every criterion, and 20 that are not, in four kinds: 6 where the chart never addresses a criterion, 7 where it raises the criterion but falls short, 4 administrative denials no chart can answer, and 3 plan exclusions (one case, case-023, was relabeled from the first kind to the second on October 30 after the archived version, with the reason under Limitations; its text is unchanged). Each template writes the chart in dictation voice, the way a clinician speaks a note, not the way a payer checklist reads, and the generator adds the routine traffic a real chart has, a referral letter, a blood-pressure check, a pharmacy call, so that about two thirds of the 19 to 35 entries (mean 25.6) are unrelated and a citation has to land on the right one. The six payers are fictional, alternating a standard and a strict criteria profile, and the criteria attributed to them were written for this benchmark from publicly described policy patterns; they are not any insurer's policy. A patient is an alias, an age, and a sex. Each case carries its grading key: whether an appeal is warranted, which criteria the chart meets, which entries support each, which entries are unrelated, and a one-line rationale. The key was written by the same person who wrote the templates, and four of its labels were wrong until the models found them (section 4.4). Read as an experiment, the thirty warranted cases are positive controls, the twenty others are negative controls of four kinds, the unrelated entries in every chart are the noise floor for citation precision, and the injected fabrications in section 2.7 are spike-ins. ### 2.4 The gate The gate is [`build/src/litmus.ts`](build/src/litmus.ts), reimplemented during the event from the published papers and not copied from any prior system. It is deterministic and sits outside the model. For each sentence it resolves the citation to one chart entry; requires the quote to appear verbatim in that entry, with whitespace, case, and quote glyphs normalized and nothing else; and requires every hard token in the sentence, each number, date, code, and side, to appear in the cited entry, the payer criteria, the denial, or the stated case facts. A sentence that fails is refuted with the token named, or, from v1.3, returned as needs-citation when every missing token lives in some other entry of the same chart. A check that throws is an error, never a pass. A draft passes only when every sentence verifies and every criterion the draft claims has verified evidence; otherwise it is blocked. The gate has no resemblance threshold and no keyword list. Its version is stamped into every verdict, and because it is a pure function of its inputs, any stored draft can be re-gated under a later version and the change recorded (`npm run regate`). The same gate runs in the viewer. Once a replay has reached its verdict, any sentence can be edited in the page, its words, its quote, or its citation, and re-checked by the gate bundled into the browser from the same module and the same admissible sources ([`build/viewer/src/gatecheck.ts`](build/viewer/src/gatecheck.ts), [`build/src/sources.ts`](build/src/sources.ts)); the result is stamped with its reason, nothing is saved, and the stored verdict does not change. It is the spike-in of section 2.7 as a control a reader can turn by hand (Figure 7). To make the module run in a browser, its provenance hash is a plain SHA-256 in TypeScript ([`build/src/hash.ts`](build/src/hash.ts)); a test checks that it reproduces every input hash stored in the result files. ### 2.5 Models, modes, and the live policy query Three models were tested: muse-spark-1.3 and muse-wonder-1.0 through the Meta Model API, and Muse Spark Open, the open-weights model, hosted on Baseten, all at effort low with eight cases in flight (three for Baseten after a run at eight lost cases to rate limiting). Each model ran in three modes. In the first the whole chart is in the prompt. In the second, the agentic mode, the model receives an index, one line per entry with the id, date, kind, and opening words, and two tools, `list_entries` and `read_entry`, and reads what it decides it needs; every tool call is kept in a trace. The third adds a tool, `policy_status`, which queries CHART, the author's pre-existing coverage index of United States payer policy, for when the named authority's coverage material last changed and was last checked. It returns no policy text, so the criteria in the request remain the criteria, and its answer is labeled as a live query against a prior-work data source wherever it appears. The viewer at [demo.hemeehr.com](https://demo.hemeehr.com) replays any case from any kept run one tool call at a time (source in [`build/viewer/`](build/viewer/)). The Muse Spark Open runs, in every mode and under the same gate, are this entry's submission for the Best Build on Meta Open Weight Models bonus prize. The agentic runs, with their tool calls traced and the live policy query among the tools, are its submission for the Best Agentic Use-Case bonus prize. ### 2.6 The advisor After the gate, a second model (muse-wonder-1.0) is shown each criterion with the quotes the draft cited for it and asked one question: do these quotes, read literally, satisfy the criterion? It answers supports, partial, or silent, with one sentence why. The answer is stored with the model's name and shown beside the criterion in the viewer. Abstract · Introduction · Methods · Results · Discussion · Live replay · Build log · Contribute


> An insurer can now issue a claim denial in about a second. Answering it takes a physician hours. In between, a patient waits to learn whether the operation their surgeon recommended will be approved or refused. > > — James H. Rosing, MD, FACS · Newport Beach, California This repository is the public record of one physician's attempt to change that balance: the evidence, the standard I believe every medical AI should meet, and the work of meeting it, measured in the open. **What this is, and is not.** The software here drafts the administrative response to a payer's denial, from the physician's own chart, against the payer's own written criteria, for the physician to read and sign. It gives no advice to patients, recommends no treatment, and sends nothing on its own. Every sentence it drafts is checked against the record by a deterministic gate before a physician sees it, and the physician's signature is the only thing that makes it an appeal. Built this week, during the event: everything in [`/build`](build/) and everything shown in the viewer. Pre-existing, not included: the author's record system, appeal engine, coverage index, and the published LITMUS standard (named in section 2.5 and the Declarations).

Fail-closed verification of model-drafted claim-denial appeals against the clinical record: a 50-case synthetic benchmark of three Meta models.
James H. Rosing, MD, FACS · Newport Beach, California · Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, October 26 to November 4, 2026
Keywords: claim denial · medical necessity appeal · prior authorization · large language models · fabrication · fail-closed verification · Medicare Advantage

> [!NOTE] > **In brief.** Nine kept runs, three Meta models, fifty synthetic denials: agreement with the grading key 45 to 50 of 50, no fabricated quote in any sentence across 17 runs, 5,824 of 5,824 injected hard corruptions caught by the gate, $0.007 to $0.054 a case, one draft passed on an unsupported case. The numbers are in [Table 1](#3-results); every table is regenerated from the result files by `npm run log`. ## Abstract The insurer has given the denial to a machine, and the machine answers in seconds. The physician has been given nothing, and must meet in hours what was done in an instant, so most denials are never met at all. The reply owed is a writ in the oldest sense, an instrument issued under a signature that binds its author to every word; a machine may draft it, but a draft that asserts one thing the record does not hold, over a physician's name, is worse than none. I asked whether Meta's models, one of them open weights, could prepare that instrument from the chart with every sentence held to the record by a deterministic check, decline when the record could not support one, at a cost and speed a practice could use, and whether the same check, pointed the other way, would hold the insurer's own determination to the same record. Fifty synthetic claim denials across eighteen high-dollar services, thirty answerable from the chart and twenty not, $940,000 of billed care, were generated with a grading key. Three Meta models drafted responses with the chart in the prompt, by tool calls, and with a live query of a coverage index; a gate reimplemented from the LITMUS papers verified every quote, number, date, code, and side against the cited entry, and 9,518 injected fabrications measured its sensitivity. Post hoc, blocked drafts were sent back once with the gate's reasons, two models ran at higher effort, and the denials were read back from letter images. Across nine kept runs, agreement with the key was 45 to 50 of 50 with no fabricated quote in any sentence; muse-spark-1.3 defended the full $568,500 of the warranted cases in each of its three runs at $0.63 to $0.96 a run; the gate caught 5,824 of 5,824 hard corruptions and none of 2,386 negation or pronoun changes, at 4 to 16 seconds and $0.007 to $0.054 a case; one draft passed on an unsupported case. One repair turn passed six of seven blocked drafts and eroded no decline; higher effort bought muse-spark-1.3 no agreement and the open-weights model 50 of 50 at medium; the letters were read with all eight fields correct in 46 of 50, every error one glyph. Pointed at the plan's determination, the gate refuted the one fabricated quote and passed a denial whose every sentence was in the record and whose reading was wrong: one chart, two verified conclusions, no side taken. The gate verifies that a statement is in the record, not that the record satisfies the criterion; the machine prepares the instrument and cannot issue it, and the physician's signature is what makes the draft a writ.
## 1. Introduction ### 1.1 The problem | Requests denied | Denials appealed | Appeals overturned | | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **3.2 million** | **about 374,000** | **about 306,000** | | 6.4% of 49.8 million requests | 11.7% of denials | 81.7% of appeals | Medicare Advantage prior authorization, 2023.[^kff] Appealed and overturned counts are derived from the reported rates. When denials are challenged, most fall. Most are never challenged, because the cost of answering lands on the people with the least time. Physicians report 13 hours a week spent on prior authorization, and 79% say patients have abandoned treatment while waiting.[^ama] The rules are not uniform. Each payer writes its own, and in 2022 the HHS Inspector General found Medicare Advantage plans applying clinical criteria that Medicare itself does not use, denying requests that met Medicare coverage rules.[^oig] The surgeon whose judgment is overridden spent four years in medical school and five or more in residency and specialty training, and carries the license, the liability, and the duty to see the patient through. The decision to refuse carries none of that weight. I do not think most of the people who build these systems set out to harm patients. But a system rewarded for saying no, and rarely asked to show its reasons, will say no more often than it should.

### 1.3 A standard, not a product

No machine should make a claim about a patient's care that it cannot support.

It must cite its source or show its derivation.
If it cannot, it stops, and the physician decides.


I wrote that standard down as **LITMUS** and published it openly under CC BY 4.0, so anyone can use it, test it, or argue with it. It applies to an insurer's algorithm as much as to mine. #### [Litmus: The Admissible Set](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21227402) Position paper · Rosing, J. H. · Zenodo, July 6, 2026 · doi:10.5281/zenodo.21227402 Generative artificial intelligence is entering clinical work ahead of any agreed method for making it safe. This paper argues that an autonomous system can be trusted only in proportion to the strength of the external check that verifies it, and that medicine has exactly one valid check: the certified specialist physician. That check has a definite shape. It returns membership in a small admissible set of treatments a qualified body would accept, a structure independently confirmed by a century of malpractice doctrine. Because the basis for membership is partly explicit and partly tacit, the machine may act alone only where consensus is explicit and settled, and must defer to the physician everywhere else. The paper sets out this method, litmus-gated reach, and the buildable system it implies. #### [Litmus: The Admissible Set (System Architecture)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21227855) Architecture companion · Rosing, J. H. · Zenodo, July 6, 2026 · doi:10.5281/zenodo.21227855 This companion document specifies the system architecture implied by Litmus: The Admissible Set. The design is one substrate applied to many workflows: a model-pluggable agent runtime, an extensible registry of standardized tools, and a fail-closed verification spine whose criteria are curated per specialty. The machine acts alone where physician consensus is explicit, routes an evidence-bounded case to the certified specialist where it is not, and records every claim, gate decision, and verdict in a provenance layer. Feedback from physician verdicts, payer adjudication, and clinical outcomes widens what can be verified over time. The document details the layers, the runtime flow, an end-to-end medical coding and appeals workflow, the build sequence from existing components, and how the architecture scales across specialties and absorbs advances in model capability.
Cite ```bibtex @misc{rosing2026litmus, author = {Rosing, James H.}, title = {Litmus: The Admissible Set}, year = {2026}, publisher = {Zenodo}, doi = {10.5281/zenodo.21227402} } @misc{rosing2026litmusarch, author = {Rosing, James H.}, title = {Litmus: The Admissible Set (System Architecture)}, year = {2026}, publisher = {Zenodo}, doi = {10.5281/zenodo.21227855} } ```

### 1.4 What is not known Large language models can write a medical-necessity letter that reads well. Whether one can write such a letter without stating anything the chart does not contain, under a check that can prove it did not, has not been measured on a set anyone can rerun. Nor has the second half of the task been measured: whether the model declines when the record cannot answer the denial, including the administrative denials for which a medical-necessity appeal is the wrong instrument. The LITMUS papers predict the shape of the answer, a deterministic check that verifies presence in the record and not sufficiency against the criterion, but they contain no measurement. ### 1.5 Objective and hypothesis The objective was to measure, on a fixed synthetic set with a grading key, whether three Meta models, one of them open weights, can draft the physician's response to a claim denial from the chart with every sentence verified against the record, decline when the record cannot answer, and do so at a cost and latency a practice could use. The hypothesis: a deterministic referential gate reduces fabricated statements in model-drafted appeals to zero on this set, at the cost of some true derivations blocked, without reducing agreement with the key below ninety percent. The secondary question was whether a model given the chart as an index and two tools, rather than whole, reads what a reviewer would read.
## 2. Methods ### 2.1 Study design and setting A bench study on synthetic data, run during the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon[^hack] (October 26 to November 4, 2026). No human subjects, no patient data, no institutional review. Everything in [`/build`](build/) was written during the event; the ledger [NEW-WORK.md](NEW-WORK.md) has a row for every commit, and the [build log](#build-log) is regenerated from the git history and the result files after every push. The line between what was fixed before the reported runs and what changed after them is drawn by the git history, not by memory. | Fixed before the kept runs began (October 27, 01:17 PT, commits `4fba43c` to `d9a2ed0`) | Changed after, each with a ledger row | | --- | --- | | The fifty cases and their grading keys. Four keys were corrected during development runs between 00:40 and 01:17 PT, each defect found by a model reading the chart (section 4.4); no case file changed after the kept runs began. | The agentic mode and its two chart tools (October 27, 20:22 PT) and the live policy query (October 27, 23:44 PT). | | The gate (v1) and the appeal contract: one citation per sentence, a verbatim quote, every hard token sourced. Fact sourcing was widened from the quoted span to the whole cited entry after a development run (00:50 PT). | Gate v1.1 to v1.5: compound number words read as one number, hundreds included, a needs-citation label naming the entry that holds a missing token, a side treated as a hard token wherever it names one, and a side word inside an idiom admitted from no source. Every kept run was re-gated under each version with the change recorded in the file; re-gating to v1.3 changed seven sentence labels and no verdict, to v1.4 none, to v1.5 none. | | The primary measure, agreement with the key, and the outcome categories. | The advisor (October 28), the mutation harness (October 28), the repeat runs (October 28 to 29), the payer-side runs (October 29, section 2.7), the viewer, and this document. | | Three models, effort low, eight cases in flight. | The repair turn and the stated reason (October 30, 23:25 PT, section 2.9, Table 5); the effort sweep (October 30, 23:33 PT, section 2.10, Table 6); the letters and their intake (October 30, 23:45 PT, section 2.11, Table 7); the compare tab and the live run (October 30, section 2.8); the dictation pipeline, proven on a text-to-speech clip (October 30, 23:55 PT, section 2.12). Every run from these is post hoc and sits in its own directory; Table 1 is unchanged. | ### 2.2 The system under test A denial arrives with its reason code and the payer's remark. The model is given the payer's written criteria, the denial, the case facts, and the chart, and asked for one of two things: a decision that the record does not support an appeal, with the reason, or a draft in which every sentence carries one citation to one chart entry and a verbatim quote from it. The gate then checks every sentence. If the record does not support an appeal, the software says so instead of arguing anyway. Nothing is sent without a physician's signature. The viewer renders a passing draft as that instrument ([`build/viewer/src/writ.ts`](build/viewer/src/writ.ts)): the payer's reason quoted at the head, each sentence footnoted to the entry, date, and verbatim quote the gate verified it against, the gate version and the input hash at the foot, and a blank signature line under a band that reads draft, unsigned, not sent (Figure 8). It can be printed or saved as text; the page sends nothing. ### 2.3 The fifty cases **What kind of denial.** Every case is a claim denied after the service was given: the payer's remittance, carrying a claim adjustment reason code (CARC) and the payer's remark, for a procedure, admission, drug, or continued stay already delivered. None is a prior-authorization request refused before care. The statistics under The problem are prior-authorization figures because that is where the public record is richest; the response to either kind of denial is the same document, the physician's record read against the payer's written criteria, and the set should be read as a test of that document, not of the prior-authorization process. Thirty-four cases carry CARC 50, not medically necessary. Three carry CARC 197, no authorization on file: in two the plan allows a retrospective medical-necessity review and the chart answers it, and in one the plan refuses that review, so a medical-necessity appeal is the wrong instrument and the right answer is to decline. The rest are experimental or investigational (56), non-covered (96, 167), diagnosis or modifier inconsistent with the procedure (11, 4), frequency (151), benefit maximum (119), and timely filing (29). **How they were made.** The set is generated, not hand-written. [`build/src/synthetic/generate.ts`](build/src/synthetic/generate.ts) builds all fifty deterministically from a fixed seed (20261027) using 18 service templates in [`build/src/synthetic/templates/`](build/src/synthetic/templates/), one per service in the table in [`build/synthetic/README.md`](build/synthetic/README.md), and a test checks that the committed files match the generator, so anyone can regenerate them with `npm run synthetic` and get the same bytes. A fixed plan allocates 30 warranted cases, where the chart documents every criterion, and 20 that are not, in four kinds: 6 where the chart never addresses a criterion, 7 where it raises the criterion but falls short, 4 administrative denials no chart can answer, and 3 plan exclusions (one case, case-023, was relabeled from the first kind to the second on October 30 after the archived version, with the reason under Limitations; its text is unchanged). Each template writes the chart in dictation voice, the way a clinician speaks a note, not the way a payer checklist reads, and the generator adds the routine traffic a real chart has, a referral letter, a blood-pressure check, a pharmacy call, so that about two thirds of the 19 to 35 entries (mean 25.6) are unrelated and a citation has to land on the right one. The six payers are fictional, alternating a standard and a strict criteria profile, and the criteria attributed to them were written for this benchmark from publicly described policy patterns; they are not any insurer's policy. A patient is an alias, an age, and a sex. Each case carries its grading key: whether an appeal is warranted, which criteria the chart meets, which entries support each, which entries are unrelated, and a one-line rationale. The key was written by the same person who wrote the templates, and four of its labels were wrong until the models found them (section 4.4). Read as an experiment, the thirty warranted cases are positive controls, the twenty others are negative controls of four kinds, the unrelated entries in every chart are the noise floor for citation precision, and the injected fabrications in section 2.7 are spike-ins. ### 2.4 The gate The gate is [`build/src/litmus.ts`](build/src/litmus.ts), reimplemented during the event from the published papers and not copied from any prior system. It is deterministic and sits outside the model. For each sentence it resolves the citation to one chart entry; requires the quote to appear verbatim in that entry, with whitespace, case, and quote glyphs normalized and nothing else; and requires every hard token in the sentence, each number, date, code, and side, to appear in the cited entry, the payer criteria, the denial, or the stated case facts. A sentence that fails is refuted with the token named, or, from v1.3, returned as needs-citation when every missing token lives in some other entry of the same chart. A check that throws is an error, never a pass. A draft passes only when every sentence verifies and every criterion the draft claims has verified evidence; otherwise it is blocked. The gate has no resemblance threshold and no keyword list. Its version is stamped into every verdict, and because it is a pure function of its inputs, any stored draft can be re-gated under a later version and the change recorded (`npm run regate`). The same gate runs in the viewer. Once a replay has reached its verdict, any sentence can be edited in the page, its words, its quote, or its citation, and re-checked by the gate bundled into the browser from the same module and the same admissible sources ([`build/viewer/src/gatecheck.ts`](build/viewer/src/gatecheck.ts), [`build/src/sources.ts`](build/src/sources.ts)); the result is stamped with its reason, nothing is saved, and the stored verdict does not change. It is the spike-in of section 2.7 as a control a reader can turn by hand (Figure 7). To make the module run in a browser, its provenance hash is a plain SHA-256 in TypeScript ([`build/src/hash.ts`](build/src/hash.ts)); a test checks that it reproduces every input hash stored in the result files. ### 2.5 Models, modes, and the live policy query Three models were tested: muse-spark-1.3 and muse-wonder-1.0 through the Meta Model API, and Muse Spark Open, the open-weights model, hosted on Baseten, all at effort low with eight cases in flight (three for Baseten after a run at eight lost cases to rate limiting). Each model ran in three modes. In the first the whole chart is in the prompt. In the second, the agentic mode, the model receives an index, one line per entry with the id, date, kind, and opening words, and two tools, `list_entries` and `read_entry`, and reads what it decides it needs; every tool call is kept in a trace. The third adds a tool, `policy_status`, which queries CHART, the author's pre-existing coverage index of United States payer policy, for when the named authority's coverage material last changed and was last checked. It returns no policy text, so the criteria in the request remain the criteria, and its answer is labeled as a live query against a prior-work data source wherever it appears. The viewer at [demo.hemeehr.com](https://demo.hemeehr.com) replays any case from any kept run one tool call at a time (source in [`build/viewer/`](build/viewer/)). The Muse Spark Open runs, in every mode and under the same gate, are this entry's submission for the Best Build on Meta Open Weight Models bonus prize. The agentic runs, with their tool calls traced and the live policy query among the tools, are its submission for the Best Agentic Use-Case bonus prize. ### 2.6 The advisor After the gate, a second model (muse-wonder-1.0) is shown each criterion with the quotes the draft cited for it and asked one question: do these quotes, read literally, satisfy the criterion? It answers supports, partial, or silent, with one sentence why. The answer is stored with the model's name and shown beside the criterion in the viewer. 24| 25|
26| 27|> An insurer can now issue a claim denial in about a second. Answering it takes a physician hours. In between, a patient waits to learn whether the operation their surgeon recommended will be approved or refused. 28|> 29|> — James H. Rosing, MD, FACS · Newport Beach, California 30| 31|This repository is the public record of one physician's attempt to change that balance: the evidence, the standard I believe every medical AI should meet, and the work of meeting it, measured in the open. 32| 33|**What this is, and is not.** The software here drafts the administrative response to a payer's denial, from the physician's own chart, against the payer's own written criteria, for the physician to read and sign. It gives no advice to patients, recommends no treatment, and sends nothing on its own. Every sentence it drafts is checked against the record by a deterministic gate before a physician sees it, and the physician's signature is the only thing that makes it an appeal. Built this week, during the event: everything in [`/build`](build/) and everything shown in the viewer. Pre-existing, not included: the author's record system, appeal engine, coverage index, and the published LITMUS standard (named in section 2.5 and the Declarations). 34| 35|
36| 37|

Fail-closed verification of model-drafted claim-denial appeals against the clinical record: a 50-case synthetic benchmark of three Meta models.
James H. Rosing, MD, FACS · Newport Beach, California · Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, October 26 to November 4, 2026
Keywords: claim denial · medical necessity appeal · prior authorization · large language models · fabrication · fail-closed verification · Medicare Advantage

38| 39|> [!NOTE] 40|> **In brief.** Nine kept runs, three Meta models, fifty synthetic denials: agreement with the grading key 45 to 50 of 50, no fabricated quote in any sentence across 17 runs, 5,824 of 5,824 injected hard corruptions caught by the gate, $0.007 to $0.054 a case, one draft passed on an unsupported case. The numbers are in [Table 1](#3-results); every table is regenerated from the result files by `npm run log`. 41| 42|## Abstract 43| 44|The insurer has given the denial to a machine, and the machine answers in seconds. The physician has been given nothing, and must meet in hours what was done in an instant, so most denials are never met at all. The reply owed is a writ in the oldest sense, an instrument issued under a signature that binds its author to every word; a machine may draft it, but a draft that asserts one thing the record does not hold, over a physician's name, is worse than none. I asked whether Meta's models, one of them open weights, could prepare that instrument from the chart with every sentence held to the record by a deterministic check, decline when the record could not support one, at a cost and speed a practice could use, and whether the same check, pointed the other way, would hold the insurer's own determination to the same record. Fifty synthetic claim denials across eighteen high-dollar services, thirty answerable from the chart and twenty not, $940,000 of billed care, were generated with a grading key. Three Meta models drafted responses with the chart in the prompt, by tool calls, and with a live query of a coverage index; a gate reimplemented from the LITMUS papers verified every quote, number, date, code, and side against the cited entry, and 9,518 injected fabrications measured its sensitivity. Post hoc, blocked drafts were sent back once with the gate's reasons, two models ran at higher effort, and the denials were read back from letter images. Across nine kept runs, agreement with the key was 45 to 50 of 50 with no fabricated quote in any sentence; muse-spark-1.3 defended the full $568,500 of the warranted cases in each of its three runs at $0.63 to $0.96 a run; the gate caught 5,824 of 5,824 hard corruptions and none of 2,386 negation or pronoun changes, at 4 to 16 seconds and $0.007 to $0.054 a case; one draft passed on an unsupported case. One repair turn passed six of seven blocked drafts and eroded no decline; higher effort bought muse-spark-1.3 no agreement and the open-weights model 50 of 50 at medium; the letters were read with all eight fields correct in 46 of 50, every error one glyph. Pointed at the plan's determination, the gate refuted the one fabricated quote and passed a denial whose every sentence was in the record and whose reading was wrong: one chart, two verified conclusions, no side taken. The gate verifies that a statement is in the record, not that the record satisfies the criterion; the machine prepares the instrument and cannot issue it, and the physician's signature is what makes the draft a writ. 45| 46|
47| 48|## 1. Introduction 49| 50|### 1.1 The problem 51| 52|| Requests denied | Denials appealed | Appeals overturned | 53|| :---: | :---: | :---: | 54|| **3.2 million** | **about 374,000** | **about 306,000** | 55|| 6.4% of 49.8 million requests | 11.7% of denials | 81.7% of appeals | 56| 57|Medicare Advantage prior authorization, 2023.[^kff] Appealed and overturned counts are derived from the reported rates. 58| 59| 60| 61| 62| 63| 64|When denials are challenged, most fall. Most are never challenged, because the cost of answering lands on the people with the least time. Physicians report 13 hours a week spent on prior authorization, and 79% say patients have abandoned treatment while waiting.[^ama] 65| 66|The rules are not uniform. Each payer writes its own, and in 2022 the HHS Inspector General found Medicare Advantage plans applying clinical criteria that Medicare itself does not use, denying requests that met Medicare coverage rules.[^oig] 67| 68|The surgeon whose judgment is overridden spent four years in medical school and five or more in residency and specialty training, and carries the license, the liability, and the duty to see the patient through. The decision to refuse carries none of that weight. 69| 70|I do not think most of the people who build these systems set out to harm patients. But a system rewarded for saying no, and rarely asked to show its reasons, will say no more often than it should. 71| 72|
73| 74|### 1.2 The public record 75| 76| 77| 78| 79| 80| 81|
82|Read the five cases 83|
84| 85|| Who | Tool | What is alleged or reported | Status | 86|| --- | --- | --- | --- | 87|| UnitedHealth (naviHealth) | nH Predict[^unh] | Predicts post-acute length of stay for Medicare Advantage patients; plaintiffs allege about 9 in 10 denials were reversed on appeal | Class action in discovery, D. Minn.; March 2026 order compels records back to 2017 | 88|| UnitedHealthcare | Post-acute review[^psi] | Post-acute denial rate rose from 8.7% (2019) to 22.7% (2022) | Senate investigation report, October 2024 | 89|| CVS Health | Post-Acute Analytics[^psi] | AI project to reduce skilled nursing spending; savings target raised to $77.3M over 3 years | Senate investigation report, October 2024 | 90|| Cigna | PxDx[^cigna] | 300,000+ claims denied in 2 months of 2022, averaging 1.2 s each | Class action, E.D. Cal., filed July 2023 | 91|| Medicare Advantage insurers, UnitedHealth foremost | Insurer-initiated diagnoses[^wsj] | Wall Street Journal analysis: diagnoses added by insurers rather than by a treating doctor drew about $50 billion from Medicare over 2018 to 2021, many of them recorded by nurses the insurers sent into members' homes; about 66,000 patients were coded with diabetic cataracts after cataract surgery, which removes the lens, and UnitedHealth members were about 15 times as likely as traditional Medicare patients to carry that diagnosis | Series, July to August 2024. In July 2025 the company disclosed that it is cooperating with Department of Justice criminal and civil investigations of its Medicare billing[^doj] | 92|| CMS | WISeR[^wiser] | AI-supported prior authorization in traditional Medicare across 6 states, including skin substitutes, nerve stimulators, knee arthroscopy for osteoarthritis, and cervical fusions[^cms] | Live since January 2026; repeal resolution pending | 93| 94|The insurers dispute these characterizations. UnitedHealth says nH Predict only guides care planning, called the Journal's analysis of its diagnoses "inaccurate and biased," and says it has full confidence in its practices; Cigna says PxDx is not AI. 95| 96|
97| 98|
99| 100|### 1.3 A standard, not a product 101| 102|
103|
104|

No machine should make a claim about a patient's care that it cannot support.

105|

It must cite its source or show its derivation.
If it cannot, it stops, and the physician decides.

106|
107|
108| 109|I wrote that standard down as **LITMUS** and published it openly under CC BY 4.0, so anyone can use it, test it, or argue with it. It applies to an insurer's algorithm as much as to mine. 110| 111|#### [Litmus: The Admissible Set](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21227402) 112|Position paper · Rosing, J. H. · Zenodo, July 6, 2026 · doi:10.5281/zenodo.21227402 113| 114|Generative artificial intelligence is entering clinical work ahead of any agreed method for making it safe. This paper argues that an autonomous system can be trusted only in proportion to the strength of the external check that verifies it, and that medicine has exactly one valid check: the certified specialist physician. That check has a definite shape. It returns membership in a small admissible set of treatments a qualified body would accept, a structure independently confirmed by a century of malpractice doctrine. Because the basis for membership is partly explicit and partly tacit, the machine may act alone only where consensus is explicit and settled, and must defer to the physician everywhere else. 144| 145|### 1.4 What is not known 146| 147|Large language models can write a medical-necessity letter that reads well. Whether one can write such a letter without stating anything the chart does not contain, under a check that can prove it did not, has not been measured on a set anyone can rerun. Nor has the second half of the task been measured: whether the model declines when the record cannot answer the denial, including the administrative denials for which a medical-necessity appeal is the wrong instrument. The LITMUS papers predict the shape of the answer, a deterministic check that verifies presence in the record and not sufficiency against the criterion, but they contain no measurement. 148| 149|### 1.5 Objective and hypothesis 150| 151|The objective was to measure, on a fixed synthetic set with a grading key, whether three Meta models, one of them open weights, can draft the physician's response to a claim denial from the chart with every sentence verified against the record, decline when the record cannot answer, and do so at a cost and latency a practice could use. The hypothesis: a deterministic referential gate reduces fabricated statements in model-drafted appeals to zero on this set, at the cost of some true derivations blocked, without reducing agreement with the key below ninety percent. The secondary question was whether a model given the chart as an index and two tools, rather than whole, reads what a reviewer would read. 152| 153|

389| 390|## 4. Discussion 391| 392|### 4.1 Interpretation 393| 394|The hypothesis held on this set. No model fabricated a quote in a sentence in seventeen runs; the two fabricated in evidence items were on drafts the model declined, and the gate refuted them. The spike-in shows why the absence is informative: every hard corruption injected into a verified sentence was caught, so a fabricated number, date, code, side, quote, or citation in a passing draft would have been found, unless the wrong value happened to appear in an admissible source (section 4.3). The cost of that guarantee is visible in the blocked column: six drafts stopped for sentences that were true to the chart but cited one entry for a fact that lives in another, or stated a count the chart never states, and two empty warranted answers stopped for having nothing to verify. The design favors blocking a true derivation over passing an invented one, and the physician is told what to fix. Agreement stayed between 90 and 100 percent in every kept run. 395| 396|The secondary question also answered itself. Given an index and two tools, the models read the chart the way a reviewer does: a third of the entries, almost all of the ones that matter, nothing at all for a denial the chart cannot answer, and nearly everything before declining a case where the evidence is absent. 397| 398|### 4.2 The disagreements, read 399| 400|- **muse-wonder-1.0 declined a wound-care case the key calls warranted.** The criterion lists infection control and glycemic management among the components of standard wound care. The weekly notes document debridement, dressings, and offloading, and the chart holds a normal A1c and a clean wound elsewhere. The model read the criterion strictly and said the record did not meet it. That is a judgment a physician could share. It is not an invented fact. 401|- **The gate blocked a true count.** "Three antianginal agents," citing a note that lists metoprolol, amlodipine, and isosorbide. The count is correct and the gate blocked it, because the number three appears nowhere in the record. The gate cannot count. Whether to exempt simple counts, with the derivation recorded, is an open question. 402|- **Empty warranted answers.** Twice in the kept runs and three times in one repeat, a model set warranted to true on an absent case with no evidence and no sentences. The gate blocked every one. That is the fail-closed design doing its job, and it is also the clearest sign that declining is the harder half of the task. 403| 404|More effort did not buy more agreement on this set (Table 6). For muse-spark-1.3 the added reasoning went into not committing: at high effort four answers set warranted to true and wrote nothing, three of them on cases the key labels unsupported, where the same model at low effort had declined with a reason. The gate blocked every one, so nothing false left, but an empty warranted answer is a worse answer than a decline, because it tells the physician nothing. For Muse Spark Open, medium effort gave the best run of any in this study, 50 of 50 with the case-023 draft declined, and high effort cost it two answers to the output cap at twice the latency. Effort low was fixed before the kept runs and stays the reported setting; these four files say that the open-weights model's five disagreements at low were not a ceiling of the model, and that one run of fifty at one setting is too few to call medium its right setting. 405| 406|The repair turn (Table 5) is the answer to the first two of these that costs nothing in the gate. Told which entry holds the number it stated, the model cited it, and six of the seven drafts blocked for a true derivation passed on the second turn at about a twentieth of a run's cost; the gate did not change and still cannot count. The seventh, the empty warranted answer on case-023, came back empty and stayed blocked, which is the behavior the design wants: a repair that argued a case the record does not support would be the repair eroding the decline, and in seven repairs none did. Seven is a small count, and the column that would show the erosion is in the table so a larger run can be read the same way. The stated reason changes nothing in the outcomes and everything in what a reader can see: with no thought text from the API, the one sentence the model writes before each read is the only account of why it opened what it opened, and in the three repair runs it never omitted one. 407| 408|### 4.3 The referential limit 409| 410|Case-023 is the most important result here, and it is on the public scoreboard rather than in a superseded run. The gate checks that every statement is in the record, not that the record satisfies the criterion. "Plan 5 to 6 days a week" answers the frequency half of a criterion and not the intensity half, and the gate passed it because the words are real. The LITMUS papers name this the referential limit: "it is a referential warrant, and it verifies consistency, not correctness." The spike-in puts a number on the same limit from the other side: 1,308 wrong values that happened to exist in an admissible source passed, and 2,386 changes with no hard token in them, a flipped negation or a swapped pronoun, passed. The advisor caught case-023 and the gate cannot, which is the division of labor the design intends: the gate answers whether a statement is in the record, the advisor offers an opinion on whether the record satisfies the criterion, and the physician who signs is the check on the second question. The viewer shows the case with the criterion text beside the quote so a reader can see the gap. 411| 412|The post hoc run from the other chair (Table 4) says the same thing from the insurer's side. The gate held the plan's determination to the same record it holds the physician's appeal to, and it took no side: the one fabricated quote in a sentence in any full run, plan-exclusion language a model invented while arguing the insurer's case, was refuted, and a determination that misread a six-visit program as short of six months passed because its words were in the record. What the gate cannot see is the flag. In the probe, a model set the denial to stand and then wrote six sentences that each support the care; every sentence verified, and only a reader can see that the letter argues against its own conclusion. The standard applies to the insurer's algorithm as much as to this one, and so does its limit. 413| 414|### 4.4 What the models found wrong with my test 415| 416|Four of my grading keys were defective, and each was found by a model reading the chart more carefully than I had. A rehabilitation chart labeled warranted documented two physician visits in 14 days against a criterion of three a week. A sepsis chart labeled absent still carried a lactate and a blood pressure in a later note. A fusion chart labeled absent still mentioned the slip and the motion on the films. A carotid chart put surgery outside the 14-day window the criterion requires. Each was fixed by regenerating only the affected cases, and the ledger records every one. A benchmark written by one person has that person's blind spots, and the models were useful reviewers of it. 417| 418|### 4.5 In context 419| 420|The tools in the public record decide in about a second: Cigna's PxDx averaged 1.2 seconds per denial, and UnitedHealth's post-acute denial rate rose from 8.7 to 22.7 percent in four years.[^cigna][^psi] The response measured here takes four to sixteen seconds and a few cents, which is the first time the two sides of the exchange have run at comparable speed. The HHS Inspector General's finding that Medicare Advantage plans applied clinical criteria not in Medicare's coverage rules[^oig] is the reason the design places the payer's criteria in force on the date of service beside the record rather than asking the model what the rules are. And the result that most changed the test, four grading keys corrected by models reading more carefully than their author, suggests a use for these models before any letter is drafted: as reviewers of the reviewer. 421| 422|### 4.6 Limitations 423| 424|- **The gate checks consistency, not correctness.** It verifies that the quoted words are in the cited entry and that every number, date, code, and side in the sentence is sourced. It does not verify that those words satisfy the criterion. Case-023 is the measured instance, and the physician's signature is the design's answer to it. 425|- **The gate cannot derive.** A count read off a list, a duration computed from two dates, or a side inferred from an entry that names it elsewhere is blocked unless the token appears verbatim. 426|- **A sentence is not checked against its own quote.** The gate requires the quote to be in the entry and every hard token in the sentence to be sourced somewhere admissible; it does not require the sentence's numbers to agree with the quote beside them. The collision class of the spike-in measures exactly this: the mutation changes the sentence's number to one that appears in the criteria or the denial and leaves the quote as it was, so about a fifth of those sentences contradict their own quote and pass. Checking the sentence against the quoted span is the next rule to add, with the derivation cases above as the cost to weigh. 427|- **Soft words are not checked.** A model once wrote "he" for a female patient and nothing tripped the gate. Sex, age, and alias are case facts and could be checked next; the spike-in gives the size of the blind spot. 428|- **One label in the key was corrected after publication.** Case-023 was labeled absent, meaning no entry addresses the intensity criterion, yet its screening note says "three disciplines at this intensity" and a progress note "the first full therapy day", lines it shares with its near-miss sibling case-034. By the key's own definitions the chart raises the criterion without meeting it, so on October 30 the label was changed to near-miss in the generator, with the reason in the case's note, and the stored result files were updated to carry it; the chart text and every verdict and hash are unchanged, the archived version carries the old label, and the one false pass still sits on this case. The counts are now 6 absent and 7 near-miss. 429|- **The counts are small, and the author graded his own test.** Fifty synthetic cases, one seed. The charts, the criteria, and the key were written by one person, which makes the test easier than a real chart against a real policy and leaves blind spots the models found four of. Six of the nine kept rows are single runs. 430|- **The data are synthetic.** No result here says anything about performance on real records, and that measurement cannot be made in public. 431|- **The denials are post-service claims.** The prior-authorization refusal before care, which the statistics in section 1.1 describe, is the same document answered in a different process, and it was not tested. 432|- **Cost and latency are the API's.** Muse Spark Open reported no reasoning tokens on the Baseten path, so its cost may be understated;[^open] latency is wall-clock from one client and not a practice's network. 433| 434|### 4.7 What should come next 435| 436|A prospective study inside a practice, under its own governance and not in public, with the endpoints that matter: physician minutes per appeal, the share of drafts signed without edit, and the overturn rate against the practice's own history. That practice exists: I am the physician who would use this, and my own practice already runs on heme ([app.hemeehr.com](https://app.hemeehr.com)) with CHART and writ in daily use, so the gate's production home is in place today and the study above waits on governance, not on building. Prior-authorization cases and the peer-to-peer. Sex, age, and alias as checked facts, and a recorded derivation for simple counts. A second seed and an independent author for the key, with inter-rater agreement reported. Real policy text from the coverage index in place of synthetic criteria. And the gate and spike-in harness used on other drafting systems, since the standard applies to an insurer's algorithm as much as to this one. 437| 438|

Conclusion 441| 442|A physician can now answer a denial at the speed and cost at which it was issued, with every statement held to their own record by a check that has not let a fabrication through in 5,824 tries. The check verifies presence, not sufficiency. The machine prepares the instrument; it cannot issue it. The physician's signature is what makes it a writ. 443| 444|

26| 27|> An insurer can now issue a claim denial in about a second. Answering it takes a physician hours. In between, a patient waits to learn whether the operation their surgeon recommended will be approved or refused. 28|> 29|> — James H. Rosing, MD, FACS · Newport Beach, California 30| 31|This repository is the public record of one physician's attempt to change that balance: the evidence, the standard I believe every medical AI should meet, and the work of meeting it, measured in the open. 32| 33|**What this is, and is not.** The software here drafts the administrative response to a payer's denial, from the physician's own chart, against the payer's own written criteria, for the physician to read and sign. It gives no advice to patients, recommends no treatment, and sends nothing on its own. Every sentence it drafts is checked against the record by a deterministic gate before a physician sees it, and the physician's signature is the only thing that makes it an appeal. Fail-closed verification of model-drafted claim-denial appeals against the clinical record: a 50-case synthetic benchmark of three Meta models.
James H. Rosing, MD, FACS · Newport Beach, California · Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, October 26 to November 4, 2026
Keywords: claim denial · medical necessity appeal · prior authorization · large language models · fabrication · fail-closed verification · Medicare Advantage

38| 39|> [!NOTE] 40|> **In brief.** Nine kept runs, three Meta models, fifty synthetic denials: agreement with the grading key 45 to 50 of 50, no fabricated quote in any sentence across 17 runs, 5,824 of 5,824 injected hard corruptions caught by the gate, $0.007 to $0.054 a case, one draft passed on an unsupported case. The numbers are in [Table 1](#3-results); every table is regenerated from the result files by `npm run log`. 41| 42|## Abstract 43| 44|The insurer has given the denial to a machine, and the machine answers in seconds. The physician has been given nothing, and must meet in hours what was done in an instant, so most denials are never met at all. The reply owed is a writ in the oldest sense, an instrument issued under a signature that binds its author to every word; a machine may draft it, but a draft that asserts one thing the record does not hold, over a physician's name, is worse than none. I asked whether Meta's models, one of them open weights, could prepare that instrument from the chart with every sentence held to the record by a deterministic check, decline when the record could not support one, at a cost and speed a practice could use, and whether the same check, pointed the other way, would hold the insurer's own determination to the same record. Fifty synthetic claim denials across eighteen high-dollar services, thirty answerable from the chart and twenty not, $940,000 of billed care, were generated with a grading key. Three Meta models drafted responses with the chart in the prompt, by tool calls, and with a live query of a coverage index; a gate reimplemented from the LITMUS papers verified every quote, number, date, code, and side against the cited entry, and 9,518 injected fabrications measured its sensitivity. Post hoc, blocked drafts were sent back once with the gate's reasons, two models ran at higher effort, and the denials were read back from letter images. Across nine kept runs, agreement with the key was 45 to 50 of 50 with no fabricated quote in any sentence; muse-spark-1.3 defended the full $568,500 of the warranted cases in each of its three runs at $0.63 to $0.96 a run; the gate caught 5,824 of 5,824 hard corruptions and none of 2,386 negation or pronoun changes, at 4 to 16 seconds and $0.007 to $0.054 a case; one draft passed on an unsupported case. One repair turn passed six of seven blocked drafts and eroded no decline; higher effort bought muse-spark-1.3 no agreement and the open-weights model 50 of 50 at medium; the letters were read with all eight fields correct in 46 of 50, every error one glyph. Pointed at the plan's determination, the gate refuted the one fabricated quote and passed a denial whose every sentence was in the record and whose reading was wrong: one chart, two verified conclusions, no side taken. The gate verifies that a statement is in the record, not that the record satisfies the criterion; the machine prepares the instrument and cannot issue it, and the physician's signature is what makes the draft a writ. 45| 46|

108| 109|I wrote that standard down as **LITMUS** and published it openly under CC BY 4.0, so anyone can use it, test it, or argue with it. It applies to an insurer's algorithm as much as to mine. 110| 111|#### [Litmus: The Admissible Set](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21227402) 112|Position paper · Rosing, J. H. · Zenodo, July 6, 2026 · doi:10.5281/zenodo.21227402 113| 114|Generative artificial intelligence is entering clinical work ahead of any agreed method for making it safe. This paper argues that an autonomous system can be trusted only in proportion to the strength of the external check that verifies it, and that medicine has exactly one valid check: the certified specialist physician. That check has a definite shape. It returns membership in a small admissible set of treatments a qualified body would accept, a structure independently confirmed by a century of malpractice doctrine. Because the basis for membership is partly explicit and partly tacit, the machine may act alone only where consensus is explicit and settled, and must defer to the physician everywhere else. 144| 145|### 1.4 What is not known 146| 147|Large language models can write a medical-necessity letter that reads well. Whether one can write such a letter without stating anything the chart does not contain, under a check that can prove it did not, has not been measured on a set anyone can rerun. Nor has the second half of the task been measured: whether the model declines when the record cannot answer the denial, including the administrative denials for which a medical-necessity appeal is the wrong instrument. The LITMUS papers predict the shape of the answer, a deterministic check that verifies presence in the record and not sufficiency against the criterion, but they contain no measurement. 148| 149|### 1.5 Objective and hypothesis 150| 151|The objective was to measure, on a fixed synthetic set with a grading key, whether three Meta models, one of them open weights, can draft the physician's response to a claim denial from the chart with every sentence verified against the record, decline when the record cannot answer, and do so at a cost and latency a practice could use. Every kept run was re-gated under each version with the change recorded in the file; re-gating to v1.3 changed seven sentence labels and no verdict, to v1.4 none, to v1.5 none. | 167|| The primary measure, agreement with the key, and the outcome categories. | The advisor (October 28), the mutation harness (October 28), the repeat runs (October 28 to 29), the payer-side runs (October 29, section 2.7), the viewer, and this document. | 168|| Three models, effort low, eight cases in flight. | The repair turn and the stated reason (October 30, 23:25 PT, section 2.9, Table 5); the effort sweep (October 30, 23:33 PT, section 2.10, Table 6); the letters and their intake (October 30, 23:45 PT, section 2.11, Table 7); the compare tab and the live run (October 30, section 2.8); the dictation pipeline, proven on a text-to-speech clip (October 30, 23:55 PT, section 2.12). Every run from these is post hoc and sits in its own directory; Table 1 is unchanged. | 169| 170|### 2.2 The system under test 171| 172| 173| 174| 175| 176| 177|A denial arrives with its reason code and the payer's remark. The model is given the payer's written criteria, the denial, the case facts, and the chart, and asked for one of two things: a decision that the record does not support an appeal, with the reason, or a draft in which every sentence carries one citation to one chart entry and a verbatim quote from it. The statistics under The problem are prior-authorization figures because that is where the public record is richest; the response to either kind of denial is the same document, the physician's record read against the payer's written criteria, and the set should be read as a test of that document, not of the prior-authorization process. Three carry CARC 197, no authorization on file: in two the plan allows a retrospective medical-necessity review and the chart answers it, and in one the plan refuses that review, so a medical-necessity appeal is the wrong instrument and the right answer is to decline. 389| 390|## 4. Discussion 391| 392|### 4.1 Interpretation 393| 394|The hypothesis held on this set. No model fabricated a quote in a sentence in seventeen runs; the two fabricated in evidence items were on drafts the model declined, and the gate refuted them. The spike-in shows why the absence is informative: every hard corruption injected into a verified sentence was caught, so a fabricated number, date, code, side, quote, or citation in a passing draft would have been found, unless the wrong value happened to appear in an admissible source (section 4.3). The cost of that guarantee is visible in the blocked column: six drafts stopped for sentences that were true to the chart but cited one entry for a fact that lives in another, or stated a count the chart never states, and two empty warranted answers stopped for having nothing to verify. The design favors blocking a true derivation over passing an invented one, and the physician is told what to fix. Agreement stayed between 90 and 100 percent in every kept run. 395| 396|The secondary question also answered itself. Given an index and two tools, the models read the chart the way a reviewer does: a third of the entries, almost all of the ones that matter, nothing at all for a denial the chart cannot answer, and nearly everything before declining a case where the evidence is absent. 397| 398|### 4.2 The disagreements, read 399| 400|- **muse-wonder-1.0 declined a wound-care case the key calls warranted.** The criterion lists infection control and glycemic management among the components of standard wound care. The weekly notes document debridement, dressings, and offloading, and the chart holds a normal A1c and a clean wound elsewhere. The model read the criterion strictly and said the record did not meet it. That is a judgment a physician could share. It is not an invented fact. 401|- **The gate blocked a true count.** "Three antianginal agents," citing a note that lists metoprolol, amlodipine, and isosorbide. The count is correct and the gate blocked it, because the number three appears nowhere in the record. The gate cannot count. Whether to exempt simple counts, with the derivation recorded, is an open question. 402|- **Empty warranted answers.** Twice in the kept runs and three times in one repeat, a model set warranted to true on an absent case with no evidence and no sentences. The gate blocked every one. That is the fail-closed design doing its job, and it is also the clearest sign that declining is the harder half of the task. 403| 404|More effort did not buy more agreement on this set (Table 6). For muse-spark-1.3 the added reasoning went into not committing: at high effort four answers set warranted to true and wrote nothing, three of them on cases the key labels unsupported, where the same model at low effort had declined with a reason. The gate blocked every one, so nothing false left, but an empty warranted answer is a worse answer than a decline, because it tells the physician nothing. For Muse Spark Open, medium effort gave the best run of any in this study, 50 of 50 with the case-023 draft declined, and high effort cost it two answers to the output cap at twice the latency. Effort low was fixed before the kept runs and stays the reported setting; these four files say that the open-weights model's five disagreements at low were not a ceiling of the model, and that one run of fifty at one setting is too few to call medium its right setting. 405| 406|The repair turn (Table 5) is the answer to the first two of these that costs nothing in the gate. Told which entry holds the number it stated, the model cited it, and six of the seven drafts blocked for a true derivation passed on the second turn at about a twentieth of a run's cost; the gate did not change and still cannot count. The seventh, the empty warranted answer on case-023, came back empty and stayed blocked, which is the behavior the design wants: a repair that argued a case the record does not support would be the repair eroding the decline, and in seven repairs none did. Seven is a small count, and the column that would show the erosion is in the table so a larger run can be read the same way. The stated reason changes nothing in the outcomes and everything in what a reader can see: with no thought text from the API, the one sentence the model writes before each read is the only account of why it opened what it opened, and in the three repair runs it never omitted one. 407| 408|### 4.3 The referential limit 409| 410|Case-023 is the most important result here, and it is on the public scoreboard rather than in a superseded run. The gate checks that every statement is in the record, not that the record satisfies the criterion. "Plan 5 to 6 days a week" answers the frequency half of a criterion and not the intensity half, and the gate passed it because the words are real. The LITMUS papers name this the referential limit: "it is a referential warrant, and it verifies consistency, not correctness." The spike-in puts a number on the same limit from the other side: 1,308 wrong values that happened to exist in an admissible source passed, and 2,386 changes with no hard token in them, a flipped negation or a swapped pronoun, passed. The advisor caught case-023 and the gate cannot, which is the division of labor the design intends: the gate answers whether a statement is in the record, the advisor offers an opinion on whether the record satisfies the criterion, and the physician who signs is the check on the second question. The viewer shows the case with the criterion text beside the quote so a reader can see the gap. 411| 412|The post hoc run from the other chair (Table 4) says the same thing from the insurer's side. The gate held the plan's determination to the same record it holds the physician's appeal to, and it took no side: the one fabricated quote in a sentence in any full run, plan-exclusion language a model invented while arguing the insurer's case, was refuted, and a determination that misread a six-visit program as short of six months passed because its words were in the record. What the gate cannot see is the flag. In the probe, a model set the denial to stand and then wrote six sentences that each support the care; every sentence verified, and only a reader can see that the letter argues against its own conclusion. The standard applies to the insurer's algorithm as much as to this one, and so does its limit. 413| 414|### 4.4 What the models found wrong with my test 415| 416|Four of my grading keys were defective, and each was found by a model reading the chart more carefully than I had. A rehabilitation chart labeled warranted documented two physician visits in 14 days against a criterion of three a week. A sepsis chart labeled absent still carried a lactate and a blood pressure in a later note. A fusion chart labeled absent still mentioned the slip and the motion on the films. A carotid chart put surgery outside the 14-day window the criterion requires. Each was fixed by regenerating only the affected cases, and the ledger records every one. A benchmark written by one person has that person's blind spots, and the models were useful reviewers of it. 417| 418|### 4.5 In context 419| 420|The tools in the public record decide in about a second: Cigna's PxDx averaged 1.2 seconds per denial, and UnitedHealth's post-acute denial rate rose from 8.7 to 22.7 percent in four years.[^cigna][^psi] The response measured here takes four to sixteen seconds and a few cents, which is the first time the two sides of the exchange have run at comparable speed. The HHS Inspector General's finding that Medicare Advantage plans applied clinical criteria not in Medicare's coverage rules[^oig] is the reason the design places the payer's criteria in force on the date of service beside the record rather than asking the model what the rules are. And the result that most changed the test, four grading keys corrected by models reading more carefully than their author, suggests a use for these models before any letter is drafted: as reviewers of the reviewer. 421| 422|### 4.6 Limitations 423| 424|- **The gate checks consistency, not correctness.** It verifies that the quoted words are in the cited entry and that every number, date, code, and side in the sentence is sourced. It does not verify that those words satisfy the criterion. Case-023 is the measured instance, and the physician's signature is the design's answer to it. 425|- **The gate cannot derive.** A count read off a list, a duration computed from two dates, or a side inferred from an entry that names it elsewhere is blocked unless the token appears verbatim. 426|- **A sentence is not checked against its own quote.** The gate requires the quote to be in the entry and every hard token in the sentence to be sourced somewhere admissible; it does not require the sentence's numbers to agree with the quote beside them. The collision class of the spike-in measures exactly this: the mutation changes the sentence's number to one that appears in the criteria or the denial and leaves the quote as it was, so about a fifth of those sentences contradict their own quote and pass. Checking the sentence against the quoted span is the next rule to add, with the derivation cases above as the cost to weigh. 427|- **Soft words are not checked.** A model once wrote "he" for a female patient and nothing tripped the gate. Sex, age, and alias are case facts and could be checked next; the spike-in gives the size of the blind spot. 428|- **One label in the key was corrected after publication.** Case-023 was labeled absent, meaning no entry addresses the intensity criterion, yet its screening note says "three disciplines at this intensity" and a progress note "the first full therapy day", lines it shares with its near-miss sibling case-034. By the key's own definitions the chart raises the criterion without meeting it, so on October 30 the label was changed to near-miss in the generator, with the reason in the case's note, and the stored result files were updated to carry it; the chart text and every verdict and hash are unchanged, the archived version carries the old label, and the one false pass still sits on this case. The counts are now 6 absent and 7 near-miss. 429|- **The counts are small, and the author graded his own test.** Fifty synthetic cases, one seed. The charts, the criteria, and the key were written by one person, which makes the test easier than a real chart against a real policy and leaves blind spots the models found four of. Six of the nine kept rows are single runs. 430|- **The data are synthetic.** No result here says anything about performance on real records, and that measurement cannot be made in public. 431|- **The denials are post-service claims.** The prior-authorization refusal before care, which the statistics in section 1.1 describe, is the same document answered in a different process, and it was not tested. 432|- **Cost and latency are the API's.** Muse Spark Open reported no reasoning tokens on the Baseten path, so its cost may be understated;[^open] latency is wall-clock from one client and not a practice's network. 433| 434|### 4.7 What should come next 435| 436|A prospective study inside a practice, under its own governance and not in public, with the endpoints that matter: physician minutes per appeal, the share of drafts signed without edit, and the overturn rate against the practice's own history.
